chapter: The banjo, rhythm and the New Orleans style
title: The figure-eight stroke he learned from Caffrey Darensbourg
summary: He explains the figure-eight 'rigamarolle' strumming that lifts a band, learned from watching Darensbourg with Manuel Perez's band.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You call that a figure-eight stroke? How do you . . . where did that come from? Is that your . . .
It’s a eight. See? That’s what that is called. Figure-eight stroke.
So that makes all those rhythms that you play.
Rigamarolle. That’s the rhythm. There’s the one rhythm. You generate. You throw a car in another shift. You’re going at ten-mile. You jump. You’re in the same position, but you generate the music.

No, I seen different bands do that around here. Caffrey Darensbourg. Seen him do that with Manny Perez’s band. You can spark the whole, you can pull the whole band, not by the tempo, but you can give it a whole lift as a feeling if you jazz that rhythm up. Banjo players could do that, because they didn’t have pianos in the band.
